blocks.x: My name is Horace White. H-O-R-A-C-E. W-H-I-T-E. That's my name, Horace White.
Let's see, and we're recording this today. This is your home where you live, huh?
Yes sir. This is my home where I live, right here. And that's my aunt. The one in the back, and that's my cousin right there. That's my cousin right there, sitting on there.
Maybe we can get him to get you an ashtray. I think he's in front of me.
Right here? No, you might not be able to reach that.
Yeah, I didn't want to. Yeah, I didn't want to mess the place up. Anyhow, let's see. It says 1842 Paulger Street.
Yes sir. Old Bourbon, huh? Old Bourbon Street.
And let's see, what's today's date? It's March.
March the 3rd.
March the 3rd of 1961. That's right. Okay, well we'll just, I'd like to get the date of your birth too, if we can.
Now, that's something I don't know because my people never did sit down and told me how old I was, you understand? And my people would sit down like y'all would. You understand what I mean?
And the time he was born, they didn't have all that you have now, like braces, you know all that. Oh yeah. But he's old enough because he's on all age with you.

You see, I didn't know my age. But, I was about, but I gave myself about 17 years old when I was, used to be second line. And I was second, and I was second line, I was second line all through you, all uptown, all through the district, all up, all up in Carlton. Wasn't a place you can call. I didn't know nothing about. But here now, I didn't say, you know what I mean? I don't mean, I don't mean in the country nowhere else, or outside, outside of New Orleans. Now, I would like, if I couldn't get me a place to be in a, you know, get me, get me a little job with some northern people, I'd be glad to get me a little job. If it wouldn't be doing nothing but sweeping, or, you know, or be a wife in the shop. Because plenty of times, plenty of times I have to wait, I have to wait so long for a little bit,
you understand? Oh yeah, you're on your old age pension plan.
Yes. But you got to wait so long before you get it, you see. So like that, I'd rather be working, you understand? Like that, I would like to be working, and have, have what I want.
Can we get your niece's name on here since you talk?
Mine? Dorothy Harris.
See, Dorothy Harris. And, uh, I'm Dick Allen. Let's get your name on here.
Oh, Marjorie Zander.
See, the secretary up, up at school, where, at Tulane, you know.
Oh, Tulane, Tulane, Tulane, that's what you see?
Yeah, that's where we work, you know. She types all this up, and I want her to get everybody's name down straight, so she can, you know, notice on the tape when she hears it.
No.
So let's see, uh, when World War, during World War I, were you a grown man then?
Yeah.
You were, you were already out working and everything, aren't you?

No, I never did work. I always did. I never did work because I had old people, or used to have, they had their own, you understand, was, was well, well, uh, well-doers, you understand. All I used to do, when they used to, I used to get money from them if I wanted anything. But I used to work, though. Like I used to, them time I used to farm brick, go sell 15 cents a bucket, or mop, or do, you know, different little job, till I make enough money. I used to make enough money to keep me going, you understand. Uh-huh. And after, then after I pulled around, I went, pulled around, I went, pulled around, selling paper. After I got through selling paper, when I wasn't satisfied to sell paper, I went and jumped on the car. See, when I jumped on the car, that way I got my legs taken off. But outside of that ship, I was all right then, man.
You were selling newspapers?

Yeah, I was selling newspaper. I was selling newspaper right there for Cora, on the next street. I was selling paper for Cora, for Ms. Cora. And all those, and then the place around here, you can call. They don't know me. White, colored, all.
I hear the musicians talk about you plenty.

That's me. And when they talk about me, that's who they talk about me. See, because all them, all the musicians from, I don't care where they're from. Mostly the musicians from, mostly they're where they leave from, from down here. And going up down, going up there and make, make a man out there self. But they don't have nothing down here. You see? You see, them time, that was two dollars a man. Two dollars or three dollars a man. For a parade, it might have been, it might have been more. You understand? For a parade, it might be more. But now for parade and fumes, well that's more, that's more. Do you understand? They give you more. Well, now out of them six men you got, no you got seven men. What six? You got seven. Got the cornet player, two cornet player, two trambone player, two mute, mute, mute. That, you know that big horn, right? That big, that big horn, well, him. They got him. After they got him, well we pays him off. Then we got, we got Ricard up here off. Now, we got Ricard. Ricard pays off. Ricard pays manual. Ricard pays big eyes lower. Ricard pays, uh, baby. And, uh, baby. And this young boy, he, in, uh, Chani. A little boy, a little drum player by the name of Chani. Used to play Chani. Drum player, used to play Chani. Well, all them, I used to be right there when he used to play, came out. I said, I said, what? Uh, they got a funeral uptown. I said, yes. I said, where at? They said, they got a funeral up on second, second and then kneel. Second and then kneel? I said, okay. I said, what horn they going to? I said, I'll tell you what you do. I said, meet me by the economy hall. Or by the person Burnton Hall or by the, or by the, by St. Dominic Hall. I said, okay. I said, all right. Now, I got to be, I'll be there, you all be there for twelve. You all supposed to be there for twelve. You all going to leave there till about. Know what time you all leave there? But one thirty. Then all you, all you all getting, all you all getting, now the Grand Marshal, all you all getting the rank with your horn and everything. You ready to pull out. You sound like you played music or something.
I used to.
What did you play?
Used to play drums.
Who did you play with?

I used to play with them little bands around, little different bands. Sometimes I used to play, sometimes I'd be short of a drummer. Man and Perez would come and get me. Man and Perez would say, all of us. I'd say, what? Come on, get your... I used to get my black. That time I used to have a black shirt, white band, a black shirt, black band, and a white shirt, and a tie, and my cap. Well, my cap used to be the old Ricker. Used to be the old Ricker band. I used to be with the old Rick in them. I used to be with all of them. Most of all of them. There ain't no place you can call. I used to be with the old Ricker band. Now, mostly, all of the musicians up the line, I know most of all of them. Some of them is dead. Some of them I done... You know what I mean? Some of them is done dead and I done forgot some of them. Some of them is dead. But outside of that, I know most of all of them. In the musicians you can call. I don't know nothing about.
What was the first band you ever heard in person that you remember?
The O'Rica. No, Tuxedas.
The Tuxedas was the oldest one you can remember?

The Tuxedas was the first one. Then come, the Tuxedas was the first, then come the Shatter Band, the O'Rica. Then after, they come, them little small, you know them little small drummers, you understand? But now all them, like all them big ones, all them, that's where they come from, them small ones. I used to be behind them all. And I don't care where they go, don't care where they went, I had to be with them. Sometimes if we play outside, if they play for, you know what I mean, for y'all. They say, Horace, I say, what? We playing for a white dance tonight. I say, all right. They say, you want, you can't? I say, it's okay with me.
You want something? I say, no, I don't want nothing.

Well, y'all, y'all, y'all, you ain't got cigarettes? I say, no, I ain't got no cigarettes. Well, y'all, y'all, y'all, go best. Go get your pack of cigarettes. Well, now when they go play, now I might not see them before, I might not see them before next week or two weeks after. But they all, they all know me, you see. Now if they don't see me, they ask her, or they ask her little boy. Or say, uh, oh, Dorothy? Oh, Miss Horace? Says, uh, do you see, do you see Horace? She said, yes. I see, yeah, no. She said, yeah, I see Mr. Horace. Mr. Horace must be at the ballroom or at the corner somewhere. Well, you, will you do something for me? She said, yes. Tell Mr. Horace I want him to be at the hall for one o'clock. We got a, we got a funeral, we got a parade. Now when I come home, I might come home, about half past two, three o'clock, or four o'clock. Now if she don't, she don't tell me, she tell her little sister to tell me. She said, Horace? I said, what? They want you for one o'clock. I said, for where? At, at the Percy Burns Hall, or at the Economy Hall, or at the St. Dominic Hall. I said, okay. Now what I do, now I get my bar, I said, Dorothy? She said, what? I said, give me, number seven cents. Alright, she said, alright, let me go look into my pocketbook and get seven cents. Now she get her cents, she give me seven cents. I catch the, I catch the bus. I used to catch a car. I catch a car and going up there. I go to the St. Leatherman Hall. See all y'all standing up outside now. I walked up in there. The other policeman, detail for the parade, you understand? Now when I walked up in there, oh, hello Horace. I said, how y'all do? I said, oh, I just said, okay. I said, where y'all going? I said, we're going to Walkerstown. I said, you going to Walkerstown? I said, who that is? Such and such a one. I said, okay. I said, let's go. I'm ready for you now. They hate it now. Boom, boom, boom. If you don't play that. They rhyme. Then they rhyme. You see, they play that. We going on up. Then we play, we play sing-on. Until we hit a block. When they hit a block, we won't, we won't, we hit it when the little drum stops.
Boom, boom, boom.

Boom, boom, boom. You see what they tell you? Six fourth time. Or eight fourth time. Well, you know what I mean? You turn your, you turn your cards over. Now you turn your cards, what's on it, you got it. And you, we gone then. Now we hit, when we hit up there, you had a policeman, policeman standing, policeman horse standing right there. I'm right, I'm right by, I'm right with you. Then he said, Peg, he says, where you going? I said, you want to ride? I said, I'm going to ride where? I said, you want to go to jail? I said, I ain't worried about going to that place. I said, I ain't worried. I said, why? I said, for what? I said, for the police, I said, for what you want to ride him for? You see? That's when you all ask him, what you want to ride him for? Well, we don't want no second hand. I want him there. He's minding my instrument. We ain't paying you for, we ain't paying you for arrest this man. We paying you to keep you, keep us out of trouble. Well, I'm coming on up with you all then, you see? I'm going with you all. Don't care where you all hit, I'm right there. Go to protection levee, go all over with you. Then come on back, come to the hall. We break up by the hall. We come in the hall. We come in the hall about six o'clock. But, yeah, but half past six, we come in the hall. Now, when we come in the hall, we break up in the hall. Now, you go to your, you know, you're going home and I come on here and watch myself. Going out in the street and go out if I got somewhere to go. I said, well, I said, well, I said, I'm not coming in tonight. I said, I tell you, I tell your mother, I'm not coming in tonight. I might come in tomorrow morning. Well, I might be out having fun, stay out all night, might stay until about twelve, one o'clock. Then I knock on the door. Who that? I said, that's me. She opened the door, come on inside. See my bride and go to bed. Now, I'm gone now. Then I stayed here for a long time. Then, out again, I'm gone. Now, I might go, might, sometime I go by the bay house. A little drummer used to be over the river. Play the bass drum.
I know him, yeah. I knew him, he died.
Yeah. Bill is good.
I know his brother.
Bill.
He's Bill's brother and, uh.
You see, he got two brothers.
He's happy. He had a brother, Happy.

Yeah. Bill, Happy, and the bass. That's only three brothers. The Matthews brothers. Yeah. I still go by, I still go by his, I still go by him here. He stays on, uh, he stays on Appaloosa Street. Appaloosa between, uh, Socrack and the Shadows Street. So I'll be, I'll be with him all. I'll be, used to be with him. Sometimes I'll go with him and sit down there and laugh and talk, have a good time with him. Sit down there. Sit down there. I used to be having a good time with him, man. Sometimes it used to be a good time for, but that's why I tell you, partner. Parade now, I leave them past. Wah! I leave them past. They ain't like they used to be. You see? I wouldn't be looking for no, them times we wouldn't be looking for no trouble. But now we look for trouble. See where I'm at now? We look for trouble. Or if I try to pick on you, I'm picking on her. You see? We're looking for trouble. The first thing you know, well, we did. You know the kid, well, who for? I look for it. But them times it wasn't like that. We're always one.
Well, why don't you talk about those times, the old times. Well, that's what I'm talking about.

The church and everything. That's what he wants to know. Well, I don't talk about all them new, all them old times. I don't talk about all that. All them music parts. I know all that. Music, all them music parts. I know all that.
Tell them how you ring the bell and everything.

Well, I used to, as far as that, I used to do that yet. I ring the bell yet. Fuel them. I make parades once in a while, but I'll be careful how I go around with them, you see? Like if I meet, I meet with Kid Alley. Or Kid Punch. Or Happy. Or anyone of them musicians. Old musicians. I know a baby. I say, what you say? Rickar says, oh, you all come hard. I say, yeah, you all come Rickar. I say, anything, huh? I say, anything up? I say, yeah, man. We got one over the river. I say, yeah. Wait on what street? Tell them, I'm gone. Be right over there. Ain't no place. I don't know where. Ain't no musicians you can't call. I don't know.
Did you ever go around to the Globe's home? Yeah. Do you remember a guy that used to play that called Buddy Bolin? Yeah, I know him.

How long has he been gone? Oh, Buddy Bolin been gone a long time. Buddy Bolin been dead a long time. You remember when he, you remember, Buddy Bolin was, Buddy Bolin died when, you remember when they killed Keith Anderson? Yeah, I've heard about that. Well, all right. He died right after he killed Keith Anderson. You remember when Chief Anderson got killed? Yeah, I remember when Chief Anderson got killed. Oh, man. You see Orlean Street? Mm-hmm. Orlean Street, that used to be, that used to be a parish. On Orlean Street, that used to be a parish. By the square? Yeah, that used to be a parish. Before they had the, before they had that tower there, that used to be a parish. The old workhouse used to be there. After they moved from there, then they moved, they built that new place on Tulane and Broad. And I know plenty. I know all of them. They know, they nothing. I don't know what, and this, and...

Do you remember that song they used to have about the downfall of the line, they called it? Yeah. Well... I think Rabbit used to sing it, the guy who played guitar? Yeah. Rabbit singing? Yeah, I know Rabbit.

Used to hang around James Alley? Yeah, I know. I used to bum in James Alley. Oh, you? I used to bum around James Alley. Eclip Alley. Mm-hmm. All around. All around up and down. Where's Eclip Alley? Right on Franklin and Gravy.
Franklin and Gravy. Yeah. You remember, you say you remember Rabbit, huh? Yeah, I remember Rabbit.

Do you remember what he used to sing? I forgot, I forgot not what he used to sing. I know he used to, yeah, I forgot what he used to sing, no. He had some song about that who killed the chief business. What's he? I forgot what kind of song he used to sing so many songs to that day too, that I didn't know what. Half of the time I didn't know what he was singing. Sometime I used to catch Rabbit. Say Rabbit, he say what? Say, you all playing tonight? Say, yeah, man, we playing in such and such a place. Say, alright. Let's call it? Yeah. Well, I get my pass. If you all playing for a picnic, I get a pass to go to picnic. Well, now, all y'all, all y'all, you, you, you, and you all, all y'all be playing and come up there. Say, sometime, sometime your, you say, your drummer get tired playing. He says, I'm going downtown. I'm going, I'm going to dance a little bit. I feel like dancing. They want to go there. Well, I take the, I snickling, take his plays, you see. I play the drum till I play the drum. Play, play all kinds. Then a piece you can call. Write a piece. Settlement piece. D-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d-d boom dear Boop Boop I said, pick it up now. You see that? That's out. I used to be on with all of them. Then I said, I don't know nothing about them. Now when you write to Louis, tell Louis harder for me.
Alright, I will.

Tell Louis I still, tell Louis I still, tell him that I ain't behind the whoop parade, but I still like to see him back here. Yeah man, there ain't no parades, nothing you can call, I don't know nothing about.
You remember the Owenwood band?
Why sure.
Who was in that?

I forgot the Owenwood band, most of all them colored fellas was dead in the hornwoods. Oh yeah. Most of all them colored fellas was dead in the hornwoods. They had a few colored fellas in the hornwoods. Because plenty of times, plenty of times, plenty of times, plenty of times Manny Perez used to play with the hornwoods. Big Iolo used to play with the hornwoods. Freddie Kepler used to play with the hornwoods. And, uh, the spell of what died there, the Piku, he played with the hornwoods. And, uh, the hornwoods. And, uh, the record, he played with the hornwoods. Most of all them colored musicians, colored musicians, played with them all with the hornwoods. And I remember when they used to have string bands. They used to have string bands. Them times they used to, you see, they used to have string bands, but alright, they used to buck between white and colored bands. See, you a white band, I'm a colored band. Now what we do, we tie, we tie a horse, we tie a, we got a wheel on a wagon, you know? We tie a wheel against the horn. And partner, and partner, wouldn't it be a shame? And partner, I whip you, I whip you all up. Then, then you come out. The same piece you play, I double it. D-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du-du And I get off it. You see, I get off my drum, then I play on my wood drum. Shiny wood plow. Boy, then we'll eat you up there after we get through. You say, I got enough, well, we all tell you that you go your way, that go mine. Well, we used to have, we used to, we used to tie up. You had a good time, too. I did one year, right after my mill and boy. We made Mazitna spit blood. That Mazitna was playing. Let's see what he was playing. Yeah, he was playing the shortest. He said, yes. Because Calamon was shining. All right. He played that. We doubled up. I said, all right. That's a white band. You're on this side. You know, you understand? You're on this side, I'm on this side. Now your horn sticking right. He's coming right to mine. You understand what I mean? You're on this side. And my horn is coming right to yours. Now. Now you might have. Ooh. Mm-hmm.

The other time, they told me about y'all. She told me that, I come last week, she says, you got somebody, one of the musicians wants to see you. I said, want to see me? I said, oh, I said, alright, I know what that's for. I said, take the record of the old time. She said, yeah. She said, do you? I said, yeah. They said, yeah. I said, yeah, that's true. I said, alright. I said, I'll be here. That's how I come. That's how I come. I said, when you first come drive. I said, Horace, somebody wants you. I said, I know where that is. I said, one of the musicians. I said, okay. I told you to come on in, so.
You were telling us out at Millenberg they were playing the Carolina Moon Keeps Shining, I believe you said.

Yeah, Carolina. . . . Booms.... DING DING DING DING DING DING DING DING Booms.... That's where you could dance at a wall or you could dance at a shardies. But mostly, most of the people who always did dance were shardies or walls. That was the walls. And shardies, they used to take that for shardies too. You see the dance would have them to. But mostly, they all would have, mostly all of them, there was a few you would catch on the floor could dance at walls, could dance at a shardies. Now all the rest of them, you know like fostry and all like that, they got them some. Like Ginnybug, you know what I mean? Take her and throw her from this way, grab her and dance with her and throw her this way and then grab her back and then grab her this way and throw her back and then grab her back and you know. That used to be like that. But, when we used to, sometimes we used to catch them like that and dance even, you see. Catch her like that and dance nice with them. There wasn't nothing man, there wasn't nothing that goes on. Shucks, I used to second line. Used to be buying everything. There wasn't nothing past me. But since, since it done start that, I don't bother with no parade no more. Now last time I made a funeral, that was, with this funeral, what I tell you about, Ricard, not Ricard, this brother was died there. Peek-coo, Peek-coo. I was behind his funeral and apparently had some people too. Don't believe Don't think they didn't. I want to touch this, to touch this one in front. The Excelsis was in the back. Now the Excelsis played all the way to the cement. Then the musicians, they went to Manalov Cemetery. The Turks onward then, they took, they got in a bus, they got in a, they had a car, well all the band got in the car, you know, and got to the cemetery where we opened up, you see, and when they brought them out, then they stayed. Boom, boom, boom, boom. Boom, boom, boom, boom. boom boom boom boom boom boom boom bamboo You stay there till we... You stay there till we close the... Go back around! Well we stay there until we close the... We can stop!
We'll stop it. We can stop it.

I thought I said... Somebody now... When we come on home then... We break up then... We done broke up then we come on home then... Then we won't have no more... Then we won't have no more fuel... Or else somebody else... Die, you understand? When somebody else die well... Well we got our... Well... I know where you stay. Alright... I'll... I'll... I'll... I'll ring up to you. Now you might be working. Alright... You're working. She gets a... She gets a telephone number. She gets a... She gets a news. I said... Tell him... I said to meet me... Time to be at the hall for 12 o'clock. Who's speaking? That's Mr. White. On the corner of the play? Yeah. Tell him to meet me for... Tell him to meet me for 12 o'clock. Alright... Well now all y'all meet... All y'all meet about 12 o'clock. Now y'all sit down there and talk... You know... Laugh and talk a while... Time for y'all to get ready to go. segments.chapter: Introduction and early life
segments.title: Opening: names, address and date of the interview
segments.summary: White gives his name and home; Allen records the date, March 3, 1961, and introduces the participants. White does not know his birth date and mentions wanting a job.

segments.chapter: Introduction and early life
segments.title: Odd jobs, selling papers and losing his legs on a streetcar
segments.summary: White says he never held regular work, farmed brick, sold newspapers and then jumped a car, which cost him his legs.

segments.chapter: Second lining and the brass bands
segments.title: Musicians know him; pay for parades and a funeral call
segments.summary: Musicians talk about White; he describes pay of two or three dollars a man, the seven-piece band and arranging a funeral parade at the hall.

segments.chapter: Second lining and the brass bands
segments.title: Playing drums with little bands
segments.summary: White says he played drums with small bands and filled in when a drummer was short, wearing the old Eureka-style cap.

segments.chapter: Second lining and the brass bands
segments.title: First band remembered: the Tuxedo and its successors
segments.summary: The first band he remembers hearing was the Tuxedo, followed by other bands; he followed them all, including to white dances.

segments.chapter: Second lining and the brass bands
segments.title: How he was called to a funeral parade and what it was like
segments.summary: White describes being sent for through neighbours, riding the car to the hall and marching out with the band to the cemetery and back.

segments.chapter: Second lining and the brass bands
segments.title: The Matthews brothers and how parades have changed
segments.summary: Talk about the Matthews brothers (Bill, Happy and the bass drummer), White visiting them, and how parades now invite trouble.

segments.chapter: Second lining and the brass bands
segments.title: Ringing the bell, old musicians and Buddy Bolin
segments.summary: White says he still rings the bell and meets old musicians; Allen asks about Buddy Bolin, whose death followed the killing of Chief Anderson, and the old workhouse site.

segments.chapter: Second lining and the brass bands
segments.title: Rabbit Brown, James Alley and a message for Louis
segments.summary: Allen asks about the song on the death of the chief and Rabbit, who sang and played guitar; White bummed around James Alley, sat in on drums at picnics, and sends greetings to Louis.

segments.chapter: Second lining and the brass bands
segments.title: The Onward band, white and colored bands, and band contests
segments.summary: White recalls colored musicians who played with the Onward band, string bands, and tying up wagons so a white band and a colored band could battle.

segments.chapter: Funerals, dances and the end of the parades
segments.title: How the interview came about; Millenberg and Carolina Moon
segments.summary: White explains how he was told musicians wanted to see him, and Allen recalls his mention of Carolina Moon at Millenberg.

segments.chapter: Funerals, dances and the end of the parades
segments.title: Dance steps and his last funeral, for Picou
segments.summary: White describes the dancing at Millenberg and his last funeral, for Picou, with the Excelsior and Onward bands going to the cemetery.

segments.chapter: Funerals, dances and the end of the parades
segments.title: Acting out a funeral parade; poor pay at home; Armstrong's letter
segments.summary: White acts out the whole parade, with the band playing hymns and blues, then says local pay is poor and relays Armstrong's letter about making money in the north.

segments.chapter: Funerals, dances and the end of the parades
segments.title: What second liners asked bands to play
segments.summary: Second liners wanted jazz and blues, not sentimental or classical pieces, and White picnic-goers are described by rooftop and decent sections.

segments.chapter: Funerals, dances and the end of the parades
segments.title: Musicians he knew: Guy Kelly, Big Eye Louis, Perez and club dances
segments.summary: White lists the musicians who knew him, praises Guy Kelly's trumpet, and describes social club dances and marching in.

segments.chapter: Funerals, dances and the end of the parades
segments.title: Crossing Canal Street, no trouble uptown, and the good old music times
segments.summary: White says nobody gave him trouble across town, Allen remembers the Young Tuxedo, and White says the old club members have died out.

segments.chapter: Funerals, dances and the end of the parades
segments.title: How club members dressed for parades
segments.summary: Club men wore a white shirt, black pants, black tie and cap for parades.

segments.chapter: Second-line identity and life
segments.title: The halls and societies he knew
segments.summary: White names the halls he frequented, including St. Dominic, Economy Hall and others, and the clubs and societies he followed.

segments.chapter: Second-line identity and life
segments.title: The biggest funeral and the bands in it
segments.summary: The biggest funeral was for a man who had recently died; only three bands were at the largest, Eureka, Tuxedo and Onward, and White names musicians who left, plus old man Glenny.

segments.chapter: Second-line identity and life
segments.title: The Robichaud band
segments.summary: Marjorie Zander and Allen ask about the Robichaud band; White knows the family, a violinist and a trumpeter, from Algiers.

segments.chapter: Second-line identity and life
segments.title: Umbrellas, cigars and his style as a second liner
segments.summary: White never carried an umbrella, as he would lose it while dancing, and carried cigars instead.

segments.chapter: Second-line identity and life
segments.title: The chief second liner: looking after children and enjoying parades
segments.summary: White claims to be chief of all second liners, tells how he brought children home safely, and describes parades in summer and winter.

segments.chapter: Church bell ringing
segments.title: Ringing the bell for the parade and tiring from walking
segments.summary: White rings the bell at his church and others, describes the echo, and how the second line went through the district; he can no longer keep up with parades.

segments.chapter: Second-line identity and life
segments.title: Singing in the second line, colored parades and musicians who left
segments.summary: White sang whatever the bands played, preferred colored parades, and says Bechet and Armstrong left New Orleans for more money.

segments.chapter: Church bell ringing
segments.title: Church bell: pay, schedule and tolling for a death
segments.summary: White explains the bell is rung for Sunday school and services, tolled for a death, and tolled every half hour before a funeral.
